controls. However, in response to the reviewer’s comment, we re-evaluated IFN-γ production by
CD127⁺ ILC1s, including under sham conditions. This analysis revealed that CD127⁺ ILC1s
exhibited lower IFN-γ production even in the absence of CLP-induced inflammation, suggesting
that this subset is intrinsically less capable of producing IFN-γ compared to CD127⁻ ILC1s (see
revised Figure 2F).
To further address the reviewer’s point, we also performed an additional analysis of the
scRNA-seq dataset. Specifically, we focused on inflammation-related genes and visualized their
expression as z-scores, analyzed separately for the sham and CLP groups. This allowed us to
examine potential functional differences in gene expression profiles between conditions and
clusters. These results are now reflected in the revised figures (see also revised Supplementary
Fig. 2D) and the revised manuscript (lines 117-119 on page 7, and lines 316-321 on page 15).
5
8. In figure 2C, the authors state that after 6 hours of CLP, number of total ILC1 increase 2-fold
(500 to 1000). In figure 3F and 3J, after parabiosis and spleen transplant experiments, the percent
of ILC1 counterpart that the authors claim to derive from the spleen out of whole ILC1 increase
from 4 to 10 percent for parabiosis experiments and 1 to 3 percent for spleen transplant
experiments. Which means that the spleen derived ILC1 cannot explain the 2-fold increase in total
ILC1 in MAT after CLP. Therefore, while it is reasonable to assert that some ILC1 migrate from
the spleen to the MAT, authors need to conduct additional experiment for explaining the 2-fold
increase in figure 2C. Moreover, since spleen-derived ILC1s constitute such a small population
of the whole ILC1 population in the MAT in both sham and CLP condition, it is necessary to prove
that these cells are a critical contributor to the phenotypes observed.
To address the reviewer’s concern that spleen-derived ILC1s may not fully account for the
observed two-fold increase in total ILC1s (original Figure 2C), we performed an additional
adoptive transfer experiment. Lin⁻ cells isolated from the spleen of CD45.2⁺ donor mice were
intravenously transferred into CD45.1⁺ recipient mice (see revised Figure 3H). At 6 h post-CLP,
the frequency of donor-derived ILC1s in the MAT was significantly increased compared to the
sham control, while a decreasing trend was observed in the spleen. These results support the
contribution of a spleen-to-MAT migratory axis contributing to ILC1s accumulation during
inflammation (revised Supplementary Fig. 3, C and D).
To more directly assess migration dynamics, we calculated a “migration percentage” for
spleen-derived-ILC1s (Sp-ILC1s) into the MAT. The migration percentage was defined as
percentage of donor-derived ILC1s recovered from the MAT relative to the total number
recovered from both the MAT and spleen: migration percentage = [number of donor-derived
ILC1s in the MAT of the recipient mouse] / [number of donor-derived ILC1s in the MAT + spleen
of the recipient mouse] × 100. The migration percentage of spleen-derived ILC1s at CLP 6h was
approximately 5% higher than under the sham condition (revised Figure 3I). While this elevated
migration percentage alone may not fully account for the two-fold rise in total ILC1 numbers, it
is important to consider that the spleen harbors substantially more ILC1s than the MAT. Therefore,
even a 5% shift in migration from the spleen could result in a relatively large number of cells into
the MAT, supporting the notion that the spleen-to-MAT migratory axis plays a key role in the
expansion of the MAT-ILC1s population during inflammation.
The exacerbated pathology observed in ILC1 KO mice suggests that circulating ILC1s play
a critical role in regulating the pathophysiology of peritonitis. However, we believe that migrated
ILC1s alone do not fully explain the disease pathology of peritonitis. Rather, both MAT-resident
and recruited ILC1s likely contribute to disease suppression. Additionally, as discussed later
(refer to page 20 of the rebuttal for our response to Reviewer #3), ILC1s may also migrate from
6
sources other than the spleen. We discuss this point in the revised manuscript (pages 16-17, lines
348-356).
9. If ILC1 are derived from spleen, authors should verify increased ILC1 circulation in blood with
markers including CD127, CXCR3 and Ly6C.
In response to the reviewer’s comment, we analyzed circulating ILC1s in the blood during
peritonitis. CXCR3-expressing ILC1s were detected in the blood under both sham and CLP
conditions (Appendix figure 1D), with a trend toward increased ILC1 frequency at CLP 6h
(revised Supplementary Fig. 4A). These circulating ILC1s exhibited low CD127 expression,
which remained unchanged following CLP. Notably, however, the proportion of Ly6C⁺ cells
within the CD127― ILC1 population increased at CLP 6h (revised Supplementary Fig. 4, B–D).
These findings support our hypothesis that CD127― Ly6C⁺ ILC1s migrate from the circulation
into the MAT during peritonitis and may contribute to the local inflammatory response.
10. FACS data in figure 2B shows that CD127+ ILC1 constitute up to 60% of the whole ILC1
population in MAT 6h after CLP. However, cluster 0 in the UMAP plot in figure 2D, which the
authors claim to be the MAT-CD127+ ILC1s does not seem to occupy 60% of the whole ILC1/NK
group, and indeed it seems to be such a small population in the UMAP plot. Authors should clarify
the discrepancy between FACS and CITE-seq data.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the apparent discrepancy between the
FACS and CITE-seq data. As shown in the original Figure 2B, flow cytometry analysis indicates
that approximately 60% of MAT-resident ILC1s express CD127 at CLP 6h. In contrast, the
UMAP plot in the original Figure 2D includes not only ILC1s but also NK cells, which comprise
a substantial portion of the NK/ILC1 cluster and therefore visually reduce the relative
representation of CD127⁺ ILC1s in the UMAP.
However, when specifically examining clusters 0 and 1, which correspond to CD127⁺ and
CD127― ILC1s, respectively, no major inconsistency is observed between the flow cytometry
and CITE-seq data. Once NK cells are excluded from the analysis, the proportions are reasonably
consistent between both datasets.
11. While Ly6C, Cxcr3, and PDL1 are emphasized as key molecules in the manuscript, the authors
do not present transcriptomic data for these markers. Providing RNA-level expression data for
these molecules would not only complement the current findings but also offer a more
comprehensive understanding of their biological significance. Furthermore, since the earlier
7
figures consistently distinguish between CD127+ ILC1 and CD127- ILC1 populations, it would
be more scientifically rigorous to compare the expression levels of these molecules within this
established framework. This approach would strengthen the clarity and validity of the authors’
conclusions.
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. As noted in our response to the comment 7,
we have provided transcriptome data showing the expression of Ly6C, CXCR3, and PD-L1 in MAT-
resident ILC1s, based on Il7r expression (⁺ or ⁻), as well as in NK cells (see revised Supplementary
Fig. 2D). Specifically, we found that relative expression levels of Cd274 (encoding PD-
L1), Pdcd1lg2 (encoding PD-L2), and Cxcr3 were high in the CD127+ ILC1s cluster (revised
Supplementary Fig. 2D). In contrast, Ly6c2 expression was enriched in the CD127⁻ ILC1s cluster
in the sham control (revised Supplementary Fig. 2D).
These transcriptomic findings support and complement our surface protein data and provide
additional insight into the molecular characteristics of ILC1 subsets in the MAT. Furthermore,
presenting these comparisons within the previously established framework of CD127⁺ and
CD127⁻ ILC1s enhances the clarity and strengthens the validity of our conclusions. These
additional data are now included in the revised Supplementary Fig. 2D.
12. The authors demonstrated the role of the CXCR10-CXCR3 axis in ILC1 migration. While
CXCL10 protein expression was assessed in the MAT, and CXCR3 expression on ILC1s was
measured in the spleen, it has not been evaluated in the MAT. Therefore, it is important to confirm
the expression of CXCR3 on ILC1s within the MAT.
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Based on the reviewer’s concern,
we
examined CXCR3 expression in MAT-resident ILC1s using the same approach as for Ly6C
analysis. We found that ILC1s exhibited high levels of CXCR3 expression not only in the spleen,
but also within the MAT and MLN (see Supplementary Fig. 3K in the revised manuscript). These
results confirm that CXCR3 is broadly expressed on ILC1s across multiple tissues, including the
MAT, supporting the involvement of the CXCL10-CXCR3 axis in ILC1 migration.
13. In lines 202-204, you said CD127+ ILC1s “drive TNF-α production” in γδ T cells through
the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway. This sentence contradicts your data and previous words in this paper.
We thank the reviewer for their careful reading of our manuscript and apologize for this error.
The sentence has been corrected accordingly in the revised manuscript as follows (page 11, line
228)
8
14. In the Extended data Figure 5 experiment, is there any data on how many adoptively
transferred CD45.2 MAT-ILC1s were in the host MAT at CLP 6h?
We do not have data on the exact number of adoptively transferred ILC1s present in the host
MAT at CLP 6h, due to technical limitations. In the generation of the PLZF bone marrow chimeric
mice, CD45.2⁺ PLZF-deficient bone marrow cells were transferred into a CD45.1⁺ recipient
mouse. Although the number of ILC1s was significantly reduced in the PLZF―/― BM chimeras,
a small number of residual MAT-ILC1s persisted. Therefore, it was not possible to reliably
distinguish these doner-derived CD45.2+ PLZF―/― ILC1s from the subsequently transferred
CD45.2⁺ ILC1s, preventing accurate quantification.
15. In the Extended data Figure 5 experiment, you used the bone marrow transfer to make an
ILC1-depleted mouse and transferred ILC1 to see the effect of the existence of ILC1. Why did you
transfer ILC1 from MAT of the CLP-induced mice? Your previous study shows that the splenic
ILC1s are migrated to MAT when CLP is induced. Transferring splenic ILC1s from healthy mice
is better to show your hypothesis. Or transplant a PLZF-/- spleen or PLZF+/+ spleen from
healthy mice to PLZF-/- bone marrow transplanted mice to see the exact mechanism of the splenic
ILC1s.
We believe that both circulating and tissue-resident ILC1s contribute to disease regulation. The
experimental design shown in the original Extended data fig. 5 was intended to assess the overall
effect of ILC1s localized in the MAT at CLP 6h (see original Extended data fig. 5). The purpose
of this experiment was not to specifically address the function of migrated splenic ILC1s, but
rather to investigate the role of MAT-ILC1s, including both resident and migrated populations,
during acute peritonitis.
To directly assess the contribution of spleen-derived ILC1s, we performed an additional
adoptive transfer experiment, as shown in the revised Figure 3, H and I. In this experiment,
we
demonstrated the migration of splenic ILC1s to the MAT following CLP induction. We have also
revised the schematic diagram and the corresponding text in the manuscript to eliminate redundancy
and improve clarity (Supplementary Fig. 7, A and F, and lines 262-270 on page 13).
16. In Figure 6, TNF-α+ γδ T cells represent only a small subset of the total cells. It raises the
question of whether γδT cells are the primary producers of TNF-α in response to CLP when ILC1s
are absent. Also, to determine if TNF-α-producing γδ T cells regulated by ILC1s are the main
contributors to preventing excessive inflammatory responses, additional experiments such as γδ
would help clarify whether γδ T cells regulated by ILC1s play a central role in controlling
inflammation in this context.
We thank the reviewer for this critical comment, which was also raised by Reviewers #3
and #4.
To more clearly demonstrate the critical role of TNF in mediating inflammation regulated by
ILC1s, we conducted an additional experiment using ILC1KO mice (NcrgreenCre x Tbx21fox/flox)
treated with anti-TNF antibody, and disease severity was assessed at CLP 6h. Experimental details
are provided in the revised Methods section (lines 390-402, pages 18-19). In this experiment. we
compared 3 groups: wild-type controls, ILC1KO, and ILC1KO mice treated with anti-TNF
antibody (revised Figure 6L). Notably, anti-TNF treatment reduced disease scores in the
ILC1KO mice (revised Figure 6M). In addition, expression of Lcn2, a gene associated with
inflammation, was elevated in ILC1KO mice, but remained low following anti-TNF treatment
(revised Figure 6N). These findings suggest that suppression of TNF production, regulated by
ILC1s, plays a key role in controlling inflammation and disease severity.
Minor comments:
1. In the supplementary figure 2A, the authors wrote the protein level on the violin plot, while the
violin plots show mRNA expression value.
We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading of our manuscript. However, we would like to
clarify that the violin plots in Supplemental figure 2A, currently Supplementary Fig. 2A, indeed
display protein levels. The axis labels and figure legend correctly indicate that the value shown
represents protein expression from data obtained by CITE-seq analysis.
2. Given the overall flow of the paper, ILC1 is the most critical population. Why are there no
marker genes distinguishing the clusters in Figures 2D and 2E?
As described above, we were finally able to define the cell clusters corresponding to CD127+
and CD127― ILC1s using the RECODE package. Application of RECODE enabled clear visualization
of the gene expression profiles of each cluster in the form of a heatmap. Il7r and Rora emerged
as representative marker genes for CD127+ ILC1s (revised Supplementary Fig. 2B).
3. In line 130, authors referenced reports on the role of IL-7 in downregulating CD127 expression,
and states that such results are consistent with their findings. Is the any reason why authors chose
the reference on T cells?
function and are considered the innate counterpart of helper-type T cells (Eberl et al., Science
2015, PMID: 25999512). Therefore, we cited a study on T cells, as ILCs share similar functional
and developmental characteristics with T cells. We believe this reference is relevant for
supporting the concept of IL-7-driven downregulation of CD127 on ILC1s.
4. Figure 3M and 3N should include data after CLP.
We have added the CLP 6h data and found that CXCR3 expression in splenic CD127― Ly6C+

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Peritonitis is an inflammation of the peritoneum primarily caused by gut perforation and consequent bacterial leakage, a known cause of sepsis. Although adipose tissue is recognized as an immunologically active organ, the involvement of adipose tissue innate lymphoid cells (ILC) in regulating peritonitis remains poorly understood. Here, we employ a cecal ligation and puncture mouse model and demonstrate that circulating CD127− group 1 ILC (ILC1) migrate into the mesenteric adipose tissue (MAT) during the inflammatory period of peritonitis. CD127− ILC1s undergo phenotypic changes to become CD127+ ILC1s, resulting in an increased number of CD127+ ILC1s in the MAT. We also show that this population of CD127+ ILC1s expresses PD-L1, exhibits low IFN-γ production, and potentially acts as a negative regulator of TNF production by γδ T cells, thereby controlling acute peritonitis. Our findings suggest that MAT-CD127+ ILC1s play an important regulatory role in acute peritonitis and may represent a potential therapeutic target for sepsis.

---

## Introduction

Peritonitis is an inflammation of the peritoneum caused by bacterial leakage from an intestinal perforation, leading to a severe acute inflammatory response. If peritonitis is not well controlled, it can progress to sepsis, leading to what remains a high mortality rate of 19.7% as of 20171–3. Despite advances in medical care, there are no definitive treatments to prevent the progression from peritonitis to sepsis. Thus, new perspectives are needed to understand early-stage inflammation in peritonitis and to develop effective immune-based therapies.

Recent studies have shown that adipose tissue, classically recognized as an energy storage organ, contains numerous immune cells; thus, it is considered an important immune organ4,5. Clinical observations have shown that mesenteric adipose tissue (MAT) accumulates at the site of intestinal perforation, indicating its role in immune regulation during acute peritonitis. However, the mechanisms by which MAT regulates immune responses during the acute inflammatory phase of peritonitis are poorly understood and require further study.

Since the discovery of innate lymphoid cells (ILC), their involvement in various diseases through the production of specific cytokines by the five subsets—ILC1s, ILC2s, ILC3s, LTi, and NK cells—has been widely studied, but their potential immunological role during peritonitis, a trigger of sepsis, remains unclear6,7. Initially, ILCs were considered fundamentally tissue-resident, but recent evidence suggests that circulating ILCs may also be involved in the regulation of inflammation. However, research into the nature of circulating ILCs and their links to disease has only recently commenced, and thus, there is a lack of insights into their involvement even during severe systemic inflammatory states such as peritonitis. In addition, recent findings suggest that ILCs interact with helper T cells, not only through cytokine-mediated interactions but also directly via cell surface molecules. The programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathway plays a critical role in immune escape and functions as an immune checkpoint inhibitor for T cells8. Although the interactions between ILC2s or LTi-ILC3s and T cells through cell surface molecules have already been reported9,10, definitive evidence for PD-L1 expression on ILC1s and their regulatory mechanisms on T cells remains largely unknown. Furthermore, while γδ T cells are known to be associated with innate immunity, how ILCs affect these cells remains poorly understood. Thus, clear evidence is needed to fill this gap in our understanding of these immune interactions.

Here, we report a immune mechanism in which MAT-ILC1s express PD-L1 and potentially suppress TNF production by γδ T cells thereby controlling acute inflammation in peritonitis. Our data suggest that spleen-derived ILC1s migrate toward the MAT and implicate a CXCR3/CXCL10 axis in this process. Our findings provide important insights for adipose tissue-targeted therapeutic strategies for peritonitis/sepsis in clinical settings.

---

## Results

Involvement of MAT-ILC1s in CLP-induced acute peritonitis
To clarify the role of ILC in MAT during acute peritonitis, we first analyzed mice subjected to CLP, a commonly used in vivo model of sepsis11. After CLP surgery, the mice had a decreased rectal temperature at 6 hours (CLP 6h) compared to sham-operated control mice (sham control), which normalized by 24 hours (CLP 24h) (Fig. 1A, B, Supplementary Fig. 1A). Consistent with this, disease severity scores indicated worsened pathology at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Meanwhile, these mice exhibited a low mortality rate (<20%) even 7 days after CLP (Fig. 1C), indicating that our CLP mice could be used as a recovery model with the strongest inflammatory condition occurring at around 6h post-CLP among the examined timepoints. Consistent with these physiological findings, the expression of inflammatory genes Il1b and Il6 was upregulated in the MAT at CLP 6h (Fig. 1D). Furthermore, elevated IL-6 protein levels were detected in both the MAT and plasma at CLP 6h, corresponding to the peak inflammatory timepoint (Fig. 1E, F, and Supplementary Fig. 1C). Additional inflammatory mediators, GM-CSF and S100A8, which are known to be involved in septic conditions12,13, were also upregulated in the MAT (Fig. 1E). In addition, similar trends were observed in the production of inflammatory chemokines, including CCL2, CCL4, CCL5, CCL11, CXCL1, and CXCL10, in the MAT at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 1D), indicating that the MAT could attract numerous immune cell types during acute peritonitis.

We next assessed whether ILCs are involved in the acute peritoneal inflammation induced at CLP 6h in the MAT. Each ILC subset was first characterized in the innate population according to the expression of NK1.1, ST2 (IL-33R), EOMES, GATA3, and RORγt, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1E)14. NK cells, which share characteristics with ILC1s, were clearly distinguished based on the level of EOMES expression15 (Supplementary Fig. 1E). Notably, the number of ILC1s significantly increased at CLP 6h, concomitant with the peak of inflammation. In contrast, NK cells and ILC2s were unchanged compared to sham controls, and ILC3s were virtually absent at all time points examined (Fig. 1G). In contrast, granzyme B-expressing cytotoxic NK cells were significantly increased at CLP 24h, suggesting a role for NK cells in the resolution phase of CLP-induced MAT inflammation (Supplementary Fig. 1F). No significant changes in the numbers of NK cells and any ILC subset were detected in sham-operated mice at 6 and 24 hours (Supplementary Fig. 1G).

These findings suggest that ILC1s in the MAT are associated with acute inflammation initiated by bacterial leakage after CLP and might be involved in regulating pathogenesis in acute peritonitis.

Identification of CD127-expressing ILC1s with a unique phenotype in MAT during acute peritonitis
Previous studies have indicated that CD127, a marker commonly expressed by all ILC subsets, is lost from tissue-resident ILC1s in the white adipose tissue16–18. In agreement with these reports, a low level of CD127 expression was detected in the sham control (Fig. 2A–C). Surprisingly, however, we observed a marked upregulation of CD127 expression on the ILC1s in the MAT at CLP 6h (Fig. 2A–C). This finding suggests the involvement of MAT-ILC1s with the unique phenotype of high CD127 expression in the early phase of acute peritonitis. At 24 hours post-CLP, CD127⁺ ILC1s persisted at a lower level, while CD127− ILC1s significantly decreased, suggesting that a subset of ILC1s remained in the MAT but exhibited altered phenotypic characteristics (Supplementary Fig. 2A).

A previous study using single-cell RNAseq analysis reported changes in the immune cell profile of white adipose tissue after CLP surgery19, however, ILC1s in the MAT have not been specifically investigated. Therefore, to further characterize the unique phenotype of MAT-ILC1s appearing during acute peritonitis, we performed CITE-seq analysis, which enables simultaneous detection of both gene and cell-surface protein expression20. By integrating ILC1 gene expression data with sham control and CLP 6h from the MAT, we identified four distinct clusters based on their transcriptional profiles (Fig. 2D, E, and Supplementary Fig. 2B). According to the phenotypes and gene expression characteristics, clusters 0 and 1 expressed Tbx21 but had low expression of Gzmb and Eomes (Fig. 2E). In addition, both clusters displayed high expression of NK1.1 and CD49a (also known as integrin α1) proteins, which are known to be expressed on ILC1s (Supplementary Fig. 2C), supporting the identification of these clusters as ILC1s15,21. Within these clusters, Il7r gene expression and CD127 protein levels were high in cluster 0, but lower in cluster 1 (Fig. 2D, E, and Supplementary Fig. 2C). Therefore, we defined cluster 0 as CD127+ ILC1s and cluster 1 as CD127− ILC1s. Similarly, clusters 2 and 3 were identified as NK cells based on their expression levels of Gzmb and Eomes (Fig. 2E), as well as surface expression of KLRG1, a marker of NK cells, and low expression of CD49a and CD127 proteins (Supplementary Fig. 2C). Intriguingly, cluster 0, defined as MAT-CD127+ ILC1s, exhibited lower Ifng expression, whereas cluster 1 showed higher Ifng expression (Fig. 2E), along with distinct variations in inflammation-related gene expression between conditions (Supplementary Fig. 2D). Previous studies have indicated that ILC1s in the adipose tissue can produce much higher amounts of IFN-γ than NK cells and play a crucial role in metabolic disorders16,17. We, therefore, assessed IFN-γ protein expression in MAT-ILC1s by comparing the sham control and CLP 6h. Notably, CD127+ ILC1s in the MAT exhibited reduced IFN-γ production, even under the acute inflammatory condition at CLP 6h, compared to the CD127− ILC1s in both sham and CLP 6h (Fig. 2F–I). A direct comparison at CLP 6h further confirmed that IFN-γ production was more restricted in the CD127⁺ ILC1 subset (Fig. 2H, I).

These findings indicate that during acute peritonitis, ILC1s increasing in the MAT exhibit a unique CD127 high expression phenotype with limited IFN-γ production.

Directed migration of Ly6C-expressing ILC1s from the spleen to the CXCL10-rich MAT
We next asked how the unique MAT-CD127+ ILC1s increased in the MAT during acute peritonitis. Given that ILC1s accumulating at CLP 6h exhibited a high level of CD127 expression, we assessed whether IL-7 production in the MAT affects CD127 expression in relation to inflammation status. Notably, IL-7 production was reduced in the MAT of mice at CLP 6h and 24h compared with that in the sham control (Supplementary Fig. 3A). Furthermore, treatment of mice with recombinant IL-7 (rIL-7) decreased the CD127+ ILC1s and increased the CD127− ILC1s population in the MAT at CLP 6h (Fig. 3A–C). These findings are consistent with previous reports showing that the expression level of CD127 on T cells is flexibly regulated by the presence of IL-7, which functions as a T cell growth factor22,23. These results thus suggest that low CD127 expression on ILC1s is maintained by the presence of IL-7 under homeostatic conditions in the MAT, and that this regulator state is disrupted during acute inflammation.

Meanwhile, if the level of CD127 expression on ILC1s was merely altered by IL-7, we would expect the total number of ILC1s to remain unchanged between sham control and CLP 6h. We, however, found a significant increase in the total number of ILC1s in the MAT of mice with CLP, while the number of CD127− ILC1s was unchanged (Fig. 2C). To determine whether this increase was driven by local proliferation or by cell migration, we next examined Ki-67 expression, a widely used marker of cell proliferation. Ki-67 expression was decreased in CD127− ILC1s following CLP treatment, whereas CD127+ ILC1s showed no significant change at CLP 6h compared with sham controls, but gradually increased during the course of inflammation, with a significant elevation observed at CLP 24h (Supplementary Fig. 3B). These results suggest that local proliferation is unlikely to be a major contributor to the accumulation of MAT-ILC1s at CLP 6h. To further assess the mechanisms underlying the increase in ILC1s, we next addressed ILC1s migration by performing heterochronic parabiosis, which allowed us to trace immune cell migration via the shared blood circulation between surgically connected mice (Fig. 3D)24. In this experiment, migration of CD45.1+ ILC1s from the intact mice was detected in mice expressing CD45.2 in the CLP-inflamed MAT (Fig. 3E, F), indicating that ILC1s infiltrate the MAT of mice during acute inflammation. Furthermore, we also found strong expression of Ly6C, known to be expressed on circulating ILC1s25, by ILC1s isolated from both the MAT and spleen under the sham and CLP 6h conditions, but not from the mesenteric lymph nodes (MLN) (Fig. 3G). Based on these findings, we hypothesized that splenic Ly6C+ ILC1s migrate into the MAT during acute peritonitis. To test this, we performed an adoptive transfer experiment, in which spleen-derived Lin⁻ cells from CD45.2⁺ donor mice were intravenously transferred into CD45.1+ recipient mice (Fig. 3H). The percentage of donor-derived splenic ILC1s that migrate into the MAT was significantly higher in CLP mice compared to sham controls, while a decreasing trend was observed in the spleen (Fig. 3I, and Supplementary Fig. 3C, D). In addition, splenic transplantation using CD45 congenic strains demonstrated a clear enrichment of donor spleen-derived ILC1s within the recipient MAT at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 3E–G). Collectively, these findings suggest that the spleen serves as one of the sources of ILC1s migrating into the MAT during the early phase of acute peritonitis.

Because splenic ILC1s showed a phenotype similar to MAT-ILC1s with high CD127 expression at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 3H, I), we next analyzed splenic ILC1s by focusing on Ly6C expression. Interestingly, we observed robust Ly6C expression in the splenic CD127− ILC1s compared to CD127+ ILC1s regardless of the inflammation state (Fig. 4A). Furthermore, the number of splenic Ly6C+ CD127− ILC1s was greatly reduced at CLP 6h (Fig. 4B and Supplementary Fig. 3J). These results indicate that splenic Ly6C+ CD127− ILC1s migrated out of the spleen via chemotaxis at CLP 6h and corroborate the significant upregulation of several chemokines in the MAT at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 1D). A previous study has shown that ILC1s express CXCR3, a chemokine receptor that mediates cell migration toward its ligand CXCL1026. Since potent CXCL10 expression was observed in the MAT at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 1D), and CXCR3 expression was detected in ILC1s from the spleen, MAT, and MLN (Supplementary Fig. 3K), we further evaluated CXCR3 expression in splenic CD127− ILC1s, along with Ly6C expression. The level of CXCR3 on CD127− ILC1s was higher in the Ly6C+ ILC1s than in splenic Ly6C− ILC1s under the sham condition (Fig. 4C, D). To further assess the role of CXCR3 in this process, we analyzed mice treated with a CXCR3-neutralizing antibody (Fig. 4E). In the isotype control group at CLP 6h, we observed a correlation trend between the splenic ILC1s and MAT-ILC1s, which was lost following CXCR3 blockade (Supplementary Fig. 3L). This disruption indicates that CXCR3-dependent migration from the spleen to the MAT was inhibited. Consistent with this, the number of Ly6C+ CD127− ILC1s in the spleen was significantly elevated following CXCR3 blockade, whereas the Ly6C+ CD127+ ILC1s were unchanged at CLP 6h (Fig. 4F). Together, these observations suggest that splenic Ly6C⁺ CD127⁻ ILC1s migrate to the MAT during peritonitis.

Since increased circulating Ly6C+ ILC1s have been reported in infection models25, we assessed blood ILC1s during peritonitis. Blood ILC1s showed a tendency to increase at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 4A). These circulating ILC1s exhibited low CD127 expression (Supplementary Fig. 4B, C), and notably, the proportion of Ly6C⁺ cells within CD127− ILC1s increased at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 4D). These observations further support the notion that Ly6C⁺ CD127− ILC1s migrate from the circulation into the MAT during acute peritonitis.

Upregulation of PD-L1 on MAT-CD127+ ILC1s at CLP 6h
Since MAT-CD127+ ILC1s in mice at CLP 6h exhibited less IFN-γ production during inflammation (Fig. 2F–I), we next attempted to identify the key factors, other than IFN-γ, regulating inflammation in the MAT within cluster 0, identified as MAT-CD127+ ILC1s (Fig. 2D, E). According to the differential gene expression analysis, Cd274, the gene encoding PD-L1, was elevated in cluster 0 compared with clusters 1–3, together with the upregulation of the Pdcd1lg2 genes (Fig. 5A). Indeed, the intensity of PD-L1 expression was highly upregulated in MAT-CD127+ ILC1s at CLP 6h compared to CD127− ILC1, whereas the level of PD-L1 on NK cells was considerably lower (Fig. 5B, C). In accordance with this, the frequency and absolute number of PD-L1-expressing CD127+ ILC1 were also greatly increased in CLP 6h (Fig. 5D–F). These results suggest that CD127+ ILC1s could contribute to immune regulation during peritonitis via PD-L1 expression.

Regulation of γδ T cells by PD-L1-expressing CD127+ ILC1s
Since PD-1 is widely expressed on T cell subsets during septic inflammation27, we considered the possibility that ILC1s might affect T cells through the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway. Next, we isolated clusters of T cells, ILC1s, and NK cells from the datasets obtained by CITE-seq of MAT-CLP 6h, and the data were applied to ligand-receptor pair analysis28. This approach revealed nine clusters according to differential gene expression: Ccr7-expressing T cells (Ccr7_T), Tbx21-expressing T cells (Tbx21_T), Foxp3-expressing T cells (Foxp3_T), NK cells, CD127-expressing ILC1s (CD127_ILC1), NKT cells, Ifng-expressing ILC1s (Ifng_ILC1), Cd8a-expressing T cells (Cd8_T), and Trdc-expressing γδ T cells (Trdc_T) (Fig. 6A and Supplementary Fig. 5A, B). Subsequently, we found that Trdc-expressing γδ T cells were strongly associated with CD127_ILC1 through the PD-1/PD-L1/L2 pathway in the MAT of mice with CLP 6h (Fig. 6B). Consistent with this finding, large numbers of γδ T cells, but not other T cell subsets, were observed with high PD-1 intensity in the MAT of mice with CLP 6h (Fig. 6C, D, Supplementary Fig. 5C). Accordingly, to validate the impact of PD-1 on γδ T cells in the MAT during acute peritonitis, PD-1 signaling was blocked by injecting a PD-1-neutralizing antibody (Fig. 6E). Adipose tissue-derived γδ T cells are known to be potent producers of IL-17 and TNF, consistent with our CITE-seq data (Supplementary Fig. 5A). We found that γδ T cells produced TNF, with levels significantly increased in the MAT at CLP 6h compared to the isotype control group (Fig. 6F, G). In contrast, IL-17A production by γδ T cells showed no difference between groups (Fig. 6G). These findings suggest that TNF production by γδ T cells in the MAT at CLP 6h is regulated through PD-1 signaling.

Next, we analyzed γδ T cells, with a particular focus on TNF production. We found that the total number of γδ T cells in the MAT remained unchanged across conditions. However, the frequency of TNF-producing γδ T cells was suppressed at both 6 and 24 hours after CLP treatment (Supplementary Fig. 5D). T cells and Macrophages are known to produce TNF during inflammatory phases29. To further assess the dynamics of TNF production in the MAT during the course of acute peritonitis, we analyzed changes in TNF-producing cells population. We found that the total number of TNF⁺ T cells and F4/80⁺ cells remained unchanged, although TNF⁺ T cells showed a trend toward an increase after CLP (Supplementary Fig. 5E, left and 5F). However, within the TNF⁺ T-cell compartment, the proportion of γδ T cells decreased after CLP treatment (Supplementary Fig. 5E, right). These findings suggest that γδ T cells are preferentially suppressed among TNF-producing cells in the MAT following CLP, supporting the notion that γδ T cells are a potential target of PD-L1+ ILC1s.

Suppression of CLP-induced acute inflammation by MAT-ILC1s through inhibition of γδ T cells in the MAT
To obtain more direct evidence of the interaction between γδ T cells and MAT-ILC1s, we generated ILC1-deficient (ILC1 KO) mice to determine the effect of ILC1s in CLP-induced inflammation. Since ILC1 development is known to be regulated by the transcription factor T-bet, and Ncr1 (also termed NKp46) serves as a surrogate marker for ILC1/NK cells, we crossed Ncr1 green Cre mice with Tbx21-floxed mice to generate ILC1 KO mice (Ncr1 green Cre Tbx21 flox/flox)30. In these mice, the deletion of T-bet under the control of NKp46 effectively ablated ILC1s without affecting NK cells in the MAT at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 6A, B). Interestingly, although the total number of γδ T and PD-1-expressing γδ T cells was not altered (Supplementary Fig. 6C, D), loss of ILC1s affected PD-1 expression on γδ T cells in the MAT at CLP 6h (Supplementary Fig. 6E, F).

Next, we used ILC1 KO mice to ask whether the absence of ILC1s affects the function of γδ T cells and regulates local inflammation during peritonitis. Notably, mice lacking ILC1s clearly exhibited lower body temperature, especially in the early inflammatory phase at CLP 6h (Fig. 7A). Furthermore, the decreased survival of ILC1-deficient mice after CLP surgery indicated that excessive inflammation was induced during acute peritonitis and that ILC1s were involved (Fig. 7B). In support of the in vivo phenotype (Fig. 7A, B), TNF production by γδ T cells was increased in the absence of ILC1s compared to the genetic control at CLP 6h, while no change in IL-17 production was detected (Fig. 7C–E), consistent with the results from PD-1/PD-L1 blockade (Fig. 6F, G). In addition, the expression of pro-inflammatory genes such as Lep (encoding Leptin, one of the pro-inflammatory adipokines), Il1b, and Lcn2, as well as levels of TNF and IL-1β protein in the MAT, and Lipocalin-2 in plasma, were all upregulated in the MAT lacking ILC1s at CLP 6h (Fig. 7F–H). These findings suggest that ILC1s prevent the exacerbation of MAT inflammation.

Finally, to confirm the functional relevance of TNF signaling, we administered a TNF inhibitory mAb to ILC1 KO mice and assessed disease severity at CLP 6h (Fig. 7I). Compared to genetic controls and untreated ILC1 KO mice, the anti-TNF-treated ILC1 KO groups showed attenuated disease severity, as indicated by lower disease scores (Fig. 7J). Furthermore, the expression of the inflammation-associated gene Lcn2 was elevated in ILC1 KO mice, whereas it remained low in the anti-TNF-treated group, comparable to levels observed in wild-type controls (Fig. 7K). These findings suggest that ILC1-mediated suppression of TNF production is essential for controlling and promoting disease resolution during peritonitis.

Additionally, we generated bone marrow (BM) chimeric mice lacking PLZF, a transcription factor essential for ILC1s development. To avoid systemic defects caused by global PLZF deficiency, BM cells from PLZF−/− or PLZF+/+ CD45.2⁺ donor mice were transferred into irradiated CD45.1⁺ wild-type recipients (Supplementary Fig. 7A). In PLZF−/− BM chimeric mice, ILC1s, ILC2s, and NK cells were markedly reduced, whereas other populations, including γδ T cells, remained intact compared with PLZF+/+ BM mice (Supplementary Fig. 7B–E). Adoptive transfer of MAT-ILC1s isolated from CLP 6h mice into PLZF−/− BM mice (Supplementary Fig. 7F) resulted in a significant increase in PD-1 expression on γδ T cells, without altering their numbers (Supplementary Fig. 7G–K). These data corroborate the observed reduction in PD-1 expression on γδ T cells in the absence of ILC1s (Supplementary Fig. 6E, F), further providing in vivo evidence of the potential interaction between ILC1s and γδ T cells via the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in the MAT.

Overall, these observations demonstrate that MAT-ILC1s increase CD127 and PD-L1 expression upon the induction of peritonitis and contribute to the resolution of excessive acute inflammation, at least in part by negatively regulating TNF production through γδ T cells.

## Methods

Mice
All experiments were approved by, and followed the guidelines provided by, the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the RIKEN Yokohama Branch (AEY2025-020(2)) and performed in accordance with Japanese law. Mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation by experienced personnel prior to tissue collection and analysis.
C57BL/6 mice were from CLEA (CLEA Japan, Inc.), and Ly5.1 mice were purchased from Sankyo Labo Service Corporation. PLZF−/− mice were kindly provided by Dr. Derek Sant′Angelo44, and Ncr1 green Cre mice were kindly provided by Dr. Christian A. J. Vosshenrich30. Tbx21 flox (#022741: B6.129-Tbx21tm2Srnr/J) mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory. All experiments were performed on 10–25-week-old female and male mice. All mice were housed and maintained under SPF conditions at the RIKEN Yokohama animal facility with a 12h day/night cycle and normal chow diet. Littermates were co-housed, and Sham- and CLP-treated animals were housed separately.

Induction of peritonitis, parabiosis mice, and spleen transplantation
Peritonitis was induced using a cecal ligation and puncture method previously reported11,45. The cecum was surgically exposed from the peritoneal cavity and ligated using sterile nylon sutures (Akiyama-seisakusyo, USP: 5-0, JIS: 1) at a distance of one-third from the end of the cecum. Next, a 21-gauge needle was used to puncture the lower region of the ligated cecum. The cecum was returned to the peritoneal cavity, allowing leakage of its contents. The muscular layer and skin were then sutured using sterile nylon sutures (Natsume-seisakusho Co., Ltd, 11mm, No. 6-0) and clipped with a 9mm AUTOCLIP Applier (Becton Dickinson). This surgical procedure was executed under anesthesia and on a 40°C-warming plate (Natsume-seisakusho Co., Ltd). Only a sham laparotomy without ligation and puncture was performed in the control group. Saline was injected subcutaneously after the surgery.
Disease severity was assessed using a clinical scoring system based on a previous report46, with some modifications. Mice were evaluated in three categories: eye opening, behavior, and appearance. Each category was scored on a scale from 0 to 3, and the sum of these scores was defined as the severity score (maximum score = 9). Eye opening was evaluated as follows: 0 = eyes fully open; 1 = slightly closed; 2 = half closed; 3 = mostly or completely closed. Behavior was assessed based on the response to tail stimulation and spontaneous movement: 0 = brisk aversive response; 1 = responds to stimuli but reduced activity; 2 = delayed response, unable to walk more than two steps; 3 = shows minimal or no movement. Appearance was evaluated based on posture and responsiveness: 0 = normal posture and responsiveness; 1 = mildly hunched posture or slightly reduced responsiveness; 2 = clearly hunched posture with delayed or weak responsiveness; 3 = severely hunched posture and no observable response to external stimuli. All scoring was conducted under blinded conditions by observers independent of the CLP procedures.
For the analysis of parabiosis mice, female Ly5.1 and C57BL/6 mice were surgically connected using the previously reported method24 under anesthesia and on a 40°C warming plate. Briefly, the hair was shaved, and the skin was cut from the elbow to the knee for exposure. The elbow-to-elbow and knee-to-knee of each mouse were ligated with nylon sutures (Natsume-seisakusho Co., Ltd, No. 3-0), and the skin of each mouse was joined. After 30 days of surgical parabiosis, the CLP procedure was performed.
The spleen of the Ly5.1 mouse was harvested, and both ends were cut to obtain the middle region. The spleen of the C57BL/6 mouse was exposed under anesthesia, and the middle region of the spleen was carefully excised to avoid damaging the visible blood vessels. The middle region of the spleen from the Ly5.1 mouse was transplanted into the spleen of the C57BL/6 mouse from which the central portion had been excised. Each end of the spleen was surgically connected with nylon sutures. Mice were analyzed 4 days after surgery.

Cell isolation from the MAT, spleen, MLN, blood, and bone marrow
Single cells were isolated from the MAT according to a previously reported protocol with minor modifications47. Briefly, the small intestine (SI) containing the MAT was first collected from mice, and the MAT was then minced in 7 ml of 4% BSA in DMEM (Sigma Aldrich, Cat# D5796-500ML) in a 15 ml tube before the addition of 100 µl of 1.0 mg/mL Liberase DH (Roch, Cat# 5401054001) to digest the MAT. Tubes were shaken for 60 to 80 minutes at 37°C, 170 rpm by Stack Shake C (Waken Btech Co., Ltd.), and shaken vigorously by hand every 20 minutes during this enzyme digestion. After cell dissociation, isolated cells were collected by centrifugation and pellets, termed stem cell vascular fraction (SVF), were suspended in RPMI-1640 medium (Sigma Aldrich, Cat# R0883-500ML) containing 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS) after removal of red blood cells with RBC lysis buffer (BioLegend, Cat# 420302). Cells were passed through a 48 μm nylon filter to obtain a single cell suspension.
For the spleen and MLN isolation, each tissue was ground on a 100 μm cell strainer (Falcon) in RPMI-1640 medium, and red blood cells were removed with RBC lysis buffer. Cells were passed through a 48 μm nylon filter to obtain a single cell suspension.
For lymphocytes preparation from the blood, peripheral blood samples were treated with RBC lysis buffer to remove red blood cells. After washing with cold RPMI-1640 medium, the cells were filtered through a 48 μm nylon filter to obtain a single-cell suspension.
To obtain bone marrow cells, bones from the forelimb and hindlimb from PLZF+/+ or PLZF−/− mice were crushed in a mortar. After treatment with RBC lysis buffer, cells were resuspended in 2% RPMI, passed through a 48 μm nylon filter, and washed twice with cold PBS. 1~3×106 cells in PBS were adoptively transferred into Ly5.1 mice to generate chimera mice, and the MAT and spleen were analyzed after 2 months.

Adoptive cell transfer of spleen cells, bone marrow cells, or ILC1s
To transfer spleen-derived lineage-negative cells from healthy CD45.2 mice, the following biotinylated antibodies were used for negative selection by AutoMACS: TER119 (clone: TER119, Biolegend), CD3ε (clone: 145-2C11, BioLegend), TCRβ (clone: H57-597, BioLegend), TCRγδ (clone: GL3, BioLegend), CD19 (clone: 1D3, BD Pharmingen), F4/80 (clone: BM8, BioLegend). After negative selection, 1.0×107 CD45.2+ Lin− cells suspended in 200 µl PBS were intravenously transferred into the CD45.1 mice one day before CLP treatment. To evaluate spleen-to-MAT migration of transferred splenic ILC1s, the migration percentage was calculated as follows: [number of donor-derived ILC1s in the MAT of the recipient mouse] / [number of donor-derived ILC1s in the recipient MAT + number of donor-derived ILC1s in the recipient spleen] × 100.
To generate PLZF−/− or PLZF+/+ bone marrow mice, 12-week-old Ly5.1 mice were irradiated with 9.5 Gy at the RIKEN Yokohama RI facility. 1~3×106 bone marrow cells from the PLZF−/− or PLZF+/+ mice were injected i.v. into the irradiated Ly5.1 recipients and allowed to acclimate for at least 60 days before i.v. adaptive transfer of sorted CD49b− ILC1s (CD45.2+ CD3ε− TCRβ− TCRγδ− CD19− NK1.1+ NKp46+ CD49b− cells) from the MAT (2.5~3×103 cells). CLP was performed 12 hr after the transfer of CD49b− ILC1s.

Flow cytometric analysis and cell sorting
Single cell suspensions were stained with LIVE/DEAD fixable Aqua Dead Cell Stain (ThermoFisher Scientific) before blocking Fc receptors with the 2.4G2 mAb (BD Pharmingen) as previously described14. Cells were then stained with antibodies for surface antigens as follows: TCRβ (FITC or APC-Cy7 or BV605 or BUV737, clone: H57-597, BioLegend or eBioscience), TCRγ/δ (FITC or BV605, clone: GL3, BioLegend), CD3ε (FITC or APC or BV605 or BUV737, clone: 145-2C11, BioLegend or eBioscience), CD4 (APC-Cy7, clone: GK1.5, BioLegend), CD8α (FITC, clone: 53-6.7, BD Bioscience), CD19 (FITC or BV605, clone: 1D3 or 6D5, BD Pharmingen or BioLegend), CD27 (APC, clone: LG.3A10, BioLegend), CD45.1 (BV421 or BV785, clone: A20, BioLegend), CD45.2 (PerCp-Cy5.5, clone: 104, BioLegend), CD49a (APC, clone: HMα1, BioLegend), CD49b (PE, clone: DX5, eBioscience), CD127 (PE-Cy7, clone: A7R34, BioLegend), NKp46 (FITC or BV421, clone: 29A1.4, BioLegend), NK1.1 (APC-Cy7 or BV785, clone: PK136, BioLegend), PD-1 (APC, clone: 29F.1A12, BioLegend), PD-L1 (BV605, clone: 10F.9G2, BioLegend), Ly6C (BV421, clone: HK1.4, BioLegend), F4/80 (FITC, clone: BM8, BioLegend), CXCR3 (APC, clone: CXCR3-173, BioLegend), ST2 (APC, clone: DIH9, BioLegend).
For transcription factor staining, isolated cells were fixed and permeabilized with the Foxp3/Transcription Factor Buffer Set (ThermoFisher Scientific Cat# 00-5523-00) according to the manufacturer′s instructions after staining for surface antigens. Cells were then stained with intracellular antibodies: GATA3 (PE, clone: 16E10A23, BioLegend), RORγt (BV421, clone: Q31-378, BD Horizon), EOMES (Alexa488 or PE, clone: Dan11mag, eBioscience), T-bet (PE-Cy7, clone: 4B10, BioLegend), Foxp3 (APC, clone: FJK-16s, eBioscience), Ki-67 (PE, clone: 16A8, BioLegend).
For cytokine detection, the single cell suspension was stimulated with 50 ng/ml of phorbol myristate acetate (Sigma) and 2 µg/ml of ionomycin (Sigma) for 90 min at 37°C in the presence of GolgiPlug (BD Biosciences). Cells were stained with surface antibodies and then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde or the Foxp3/Transcription Factor Buffer Set after two washes with PBS. Fluorochrome-conjugated intracellular antibodies IFN-γ (FITC or BV421, clone: XMG1.2, BioLegend), TNF-α (PE or APC, clone: MP6-XT22, BioLegend or eBioscience) or IL-17A (APC or PE-Cy7, clone: TC11-18H10.1, BioLegend) were diluted in 1x Perm buffer provided from the Foxp3/Transcription Factor Buffer Set and stained for 60 min at 4°C.
For identification of ILC subsets, NK cells were defined as CD45.2+ CD3ε− TCRβ− TCRγδ− CD19− RORγt− NK1.1+ EOMES+, ILC1s as CD45.2+ CD3ε− TCRβ− TCRγδ− CD19− RORγt− NK1.1+ EOMES−, ILC2s as CD45.2+ TCRβ− CD3ε− CD19− RORγt− Gata3+ ST2+, and ILC3s as CD45.2+ TCRβ− CD3ε− CD19− RORγt+. For lymphocyte analysis, cells were first strictly defined by forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) parameters, followed by gating on live cells for each analysis.
All stained cells were analyzed or sorted on BD FACSAria III or BD LSRFortessa X-20 Cell analyzer, and the data obtained were analyzed using FlowJo v10.8.1 (BD Biosciences).
All FACS antibodies used in this study, including catalogue numbers and staining dilutions, are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Cytokine and chemokine measurements in MAT and plasma
MAT was collected and crushed using the SK-miru (TOKKEN, Inc.) in liquid nitrogen after weight adjustment, and diluted RIPA buffer (Merck, Cat# 20-188) was used to lyse the crushed MAT. The tubes were then placed on ice for 3 h and mixed by vortexing every hour. After centrifugation at maximum speed, the resulting tissues were discarded, and the supernatant was transferred to new tubes; this step was repeated 3 times. After the last step, the supernatant was aliquoted and stored at −20°C until the analysis. Whole blood samples were collected from each mouse, and plasma was prepared by centrifugation. An ELISA assay was performed to evaluate IL-7 (R&D system, DY407), Lipocalin-2 (R&D system, MLCN20), IL-1β (BioLegend, 432604), and TNF-α (R&D system, MHSTA50). Cytometric Beads Array (BD Pharmingen) was used for IL-6 measurement, and Luminex assay systems (LXSAMSM-33, LXSAMSM-03, and LXSAMSM-01) were also performed for the comprehensive analysis of cytokines and chemokines in the MAT according to the manufacturer′s protocol. All samples were stored at −20°C until the analysis.

Administration of recombinant proteins, anti-CXCR3 antibody, anti-PD-1 antibody, and anti-TNF antibody
5 µg of recombinant IL-7 (BioLegend, Cat# 577804) in 200 µl PBS was administered i.p. 1 day before CLP and then again i.v. after CLP. Control mice were treated with PBS only at the same time points.
For in vivo antibody treatment, 200 µg of monoclonal anti-CXCR3 antibody (BioXcell, clone: CXCR3-173, Cat# BE0249), 250 µg of monoclonal anti-PD-1 antibody (BioLegend, clone: 29F.1A12, Cat# 135247), or 250 µg of monoclonal anti-TNFα antibody (BioXcell, clone: XT3.11, Cat# BE0058) in 200 µl PBS was administered intraperitoneally 3 days and 1 day prior to CLP, and intravenously immediately after CLP. Control mice were given the same volume of hamster IgG (BioXcell, Cat# BE0091), Rat IgG2a, k (BioLegend, Cat# 400565), or Rat IgG1 (BioXcell, Cat# BE0088).

Gene analysis by CITE-seq
For CITE seq library preparation, SVF single cells isolated from the MAT of each mouse group were stained with TotalSeq B antibodies (BioLegend) after blocking with Fc receptor (2.4G2) as follows: I-A/I-E (clone: M5/114.15.2), CD19 (clone: 6D5), CD27 (clone: LG.3A10), CD45.2 (clone: 104), CD49a (clone: HMa1), CD127 (clone: A7R34), FcεR1 (clone: 1-Mar), KLRG1 (clone: 2F1/KLRG1), Ly6C (clone: HK1.4), NK1.1 (clone: PK136), TCRβ (clone: H57-597), PD-1 (clone: RMP1-30), PD-L1 (clone: MIH6), Rat IgG2ak (clone: 400581), Rat IgG2bk (clone: RTK4530). After staining, the lymphocyte fraction, gated on SSC vs FSC, excluding the dead cells stained with PI, was sorted before passing through the 10X chromium controller to generate the droplets.
The library was generated according to the protocol of Chromium Next Gem Single Cell 3ʹ Reagent Kits v3.1. Each library was sequenced using Hiseq X (Illumina). All TotalSeq B antibodies used in this study, including catalogue numbers and staining dilutions, are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

Clustering and gene expression analysis with Seurat and CellphoneDB
Demultiplexing and UMI counting of each FASTA file was performed using the Cell Ranger pipeline (https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-gene-expression/software/pipelines/latest/using/tutorials) and the files 'barcodes.tsv, features.tsv and matrix.mtx were generated using the mouse genome reference mm10. These files were imported into RStudio, and the Seurat objects were created using the R package Seurat v4.0 and analyzed as described below using the Seurat tutorial (https://satijalab.org/seurat/)48. Cells containing more than 10% of mitochondrial genes were removed as dead cells. To visualize and identify the clusters, dimensional reduction was performed using UMAP after scaling the data, and each cluster was characterized based on cluster-specific gene and protein expression. ILC1/NK clusters were extracted from all clusters based on protein expression of NK1.1 > 0.5, TCRβ < 0.5, and CD19 < 0.5, and gene expression Cd3e < 0.5, then re-clustered. After sub-clustering, both Seurat object sham control and CLP 6h were integrated using canonical correlation analysis (CCA).
Gene expression analysis was performed according to the Seurat protocol using the “FindMakers” function, with or without RECODE reprocessing (https://yusukeimoto.github.io/images/RECODE_R_Tutorials/Run_RECODE_on_R_tutorial.html)49. Gene and protein expression information was visualized in volcanoplots and violin plots.
For cell-cell interaction analysis, CellPhoneDB v2.0 was used for ligand-receptor pairs analysis28. To understand the interaction of T cells and ILC1 at CLP 6h and above, ILC1/NK and T cell clusters were extracted from all Seurat clusters of the CLP 6h dataset as ILC1/NK/T cell-Seurat objects. Then, count data and metadata were obtained from the ILC1/NK/T cell-Seurat object and the ensemble symbol of mouse was changed to that of human, because CellPhoneDB only accepts the human symbol for analysis. Using the count and metadata files, ligand-receptor pairs and cluster pairs that interact with each other were identified and visualized as heatmaps and bubble plots, using the Python 3 pipeline, following the CellPhoneDB tutorial.

RNA extraction and quantitative PCR analysis
5 mm of the MAT was frozen and crushed using the SK-miru (Tokken, Inc.) in liquid nitrogen after washing with PBS. The crushed tissues were then lysed in RLT buffer (QIAGEN, Cat# 74106) containing 2-mercaptoethanol (Nacalai Tesque, Cat# 21438-82). The RNeasy Mini Kit (QIAGEN, Cat# 74106) was used for total RNA extraction according to the manufacturer′s instructions. Isolated RNAs were then converted to cDNAs by RiverTra Ace (TOYOBO, Cat# TRF-101) using random primers (TOYOBO, Cat# FSK-301). Quantitative PCR was performed using the SYBR Premix Ex Taq (Takara, Cat# RR820L) on a LightCycler 480 (Roche) or Thermal Cycler Dice TP800 (Takara Bio Inc.) with the following primers. Hprt50: Fw, 5′-CCTAAGATGAGCGCAAGTTGAA-3′, Rv, 5′-CCACAGGACTAGAACACCTGCTAA-3′; Il6: Fw, 5′-ATGGATGCTACCAAACTGGAT-3′, Rv, 5′-TGAAGGACTCTGGCTTTGTCT-3′; Il1b51: Fw, 5′-CGACAAAATACCTGTGGCCT-3′, Rv, 5′-TTCTTTGGGTATTGCTTGGG-3′; Lep: Fw, 5′-GCAAGAAGAAGAAGATCCCAGG-3′, Rv, 5′-CAGATAGGACCAAAGCCACAG-3′; Lcn2: Fw, 5′-TGGCCACTTGCACATTGTAG-3′, Rv, 5′-ATGTCACCTCCATCCTGGTC-3′.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis and visualization of results were conducted using Prism v.9 or R v4.2.1. Biological represented data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Outliers were identified and excluded using Tukey′s method implemented in GraphPad Prism. Data were tested for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test prior to statistical analysis. For normally distributed data, statistically significant differences between two groups were detected by two-tailed Student′s t test, among multiple groups using one-way ANOVA with Tuky′s-test. For non-parametric data, the Mann–Whitney U test or Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn′s multiple comparison test was used. Differences between groups classified by two independent factors were detected by two-way ANOVA with Sidak′s test. For the gene expression analysis in the CITE-seq data, MAST was selected in the Seurat command ‘FindMakers’ to detect the significance52.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript entitled, “PD-L1 expressing CD127+ ILC1s inhibit PD-1+ γδ T cells in the mesenteric adipose tissue to alleviate murine peritonitis” reports the role of crosstalk between mesenteric adipose tissue (MAT)-CD127+ILC1s and γδ T cells through the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in controlling CLP-induced acute peritonitis by suppressing excessive inflammation. In this article, the authors showed that ILC1 expressing high levels of IL-7Ra (CD127) are increased during acute peritonitis, and they suppress the TNFa+ gamma delta T cell function via direct contact with the cells via PD-L1 and PD-1 interaction. The authors showed that those ILC1s originated from the spleen, and were recruited to mesenteric adipose tissue via CXCR3 – CXCL10 axis. The authors performed various robust experiments and tried to discover the systemic and cellular mechanism for regulating inflammatory gamma delta T cells via ILC1s. While most of the conclusions are well supported by convincing data, additional experiments and appropriate control should be performed and included to further strengthen the manuscript.

Major comments:
1. The authors utilized CLP as an inducer of peritonitis. This model naturally progresses to sepsis, leading to mortality in the mice. Depending on the severity of CLP, it appears to influence the degree of temperature drop and the time required for recovery. The authors specifically focus on peritonitis, as mentioned in the title of the paper. According to the Methods section, the authors performed a 0.5 cm cecal exposure, which corresponds to a moderate CLP induction. However, the more significant temperature changes seem to occur at later time points, such as 8 and 12 hours, rather than at 6 hours. Therefore, further explanation is needed as to why the authors chose to focus on the 6-hour time point.
2. Moreover, the differences in survival observed in the later stages of the study are ultimately related to the effects of sepsis. If the authors aim to focus on peritonitis, they should demonstrate changes in phenotypes other than temperature to justify their discussion of the immune response to peritonitis.
3. The authors claimed that mesenteric adipose tissue (MAT) ILC1 is associated with acute peritonitis (line 81-83). As a reason for the claim, the authors showed the increased cell number in ILC1, while the number of other ILCs or NK cells did not increase. However, the absolute cell number of ILC1 is lower than NK cells or ILC2. Furthermore, the authors did not show the number of peritoneal myeloid cells, such as macrophages and neutrophils, which are abundant in peritoneal cavity and participate in inflammatory pathways such as acute peritonitis. Understanding the relative abundance of ILCs among other immune cells could provide important context for their role in the immune response. The authors need to sufficiently explain why they focus on ILCs over the many other types of infiltrating immune cells. There are some models to specifically deplete ILCs while sustaining T cell functionality (Rafei-Shamsabadi, D, A. Lack of Type 2 Innate Lymphoid Cells Promotes a Type I-Driven Enhanced Immune Response in Contact Hypersensitivity. J Invest Dermatol (2018)). If the authors have performed such a specific ILC depletion, then the importance of ILCs will be highlighted.

However, in the violin plot, cluster1 expressed the highest level of T-bet (Tbx21) and IFN-gamma (Ifng). Therefore, rather than a mere mixture of cells, the cluster is a specific cluster with specific gene expression. 5. In both the Figure 2E and Extended Data Figure 2A legends, it is clear that the same dataset was used. The CITE-seq results refer to the ILC1/NK population. For more accurate analysis, it would be better to first distinguish ILC1 and NK cells based on EOMES expression. Following this, the ILC1 population could be further subdivided according to CD127 expression levels for a more precise assessment of IFN-γ production in each group.
7. I wonder why there is no analysis of CD127+ ILC1 in the sham group in Figure 2F. It would be interesting to know if CD127+ ILC1 show not only numerical differences in the CLP group but also changes in functional characteristics such as IFN-γ expression, or if CD127+ ILC1 inherently produce low levels of IFN-γ, regardless of CLP. Additionally, investigating the differences in cell characteristics between these groups could be further explored by performing a more detailed analysis of the single cell analysis data from Figure 2D, separating the Sham and CLP groups.

In figure 3F and 3J, after parabiosis and spleen transplant experiments, the percent of ILC1 counterpart that the authors claim to derive from the spleen out of whole ILC1 increase from 4 to 10 percent for parabiosis experiments and 1 to 3 percent for spleen transplant experiments. Which means that the spleen derived ILC1 cannot explain the 2-fold increase in total ILC1 in MAT after CLP. Therefore, while it is reasonable to assert that some ILC1 migrate from the spleen to the MAT, authors need to conduct additional experiment for explaining the 2-fold increase in figure 2C. 11. While Ly6C, Cxcr3, and PDL1 are emphasized as key molecules in the manuscript, the authors do not present transcriptomic data for these markers. Providing RNA-level expression data for these molecules would not only complement the current findings but also offer a more comprehensive understanding of their biological significance. Furthermore, since the earlier figures consistently distinguish between CD127+ ILC1 and CD127- ILC1 populations, it would be more scientifically rigorous to compare the expression levels of these molecules within this established framework. ### Reviewer 3

In the present manuscript Nagata et al investigated the role of ILC1s during peritonitis, by using a model of cecal ligation and puncture (CLP). The authors show that upon inflammation the numbers of ILC1s transiently increase in the mesenteric adipose tissue (MAT), alongside their expression of CD127. These cells possess a unique phenotype producing less IFNg than their CD127- counterparts and expressing high levels of PD-L1, suggestive of a regulatory role. Indeed the authors show that genetic ablation of ILC1s induces increased inflammation, as evidenced by more TNF production by gd T cells and decreased body temperature, ultimately decreasing survival of the animals. Interestingly, the authors suggest that these "regulatory" ILC1s migrate from the spleen to the MAT in a CXCR3-dependent manner. The findings presented here are novel and part of them are supported by very elegant approaches. In my opinion, however, this manuscript would benefit from additional experiments to strengthen the authors' claims, as delineated below.

Major points:
- Even though Nagata et al used very interesting approaches to pinpoint a role for migration in the ILC1 response during CLP (such as spleen transplants and parabiosis), I think some key points need to be addressed. First, in Figure 1h, we observe that the numbers of ILC1 double at 6h post CLP, however, in both the parabiosis and transplantation experiments, the frequency of ILC1s coming from circulation is less than 10% (9% and 5% on average, respectively). Have the authors checked for local proliferation? Also, could these ILC1s coming from other tissues such as the liver and gut? Upon CXCR3 blockade the authors observe an enrichment in ILC1s in the Spleen (suggesting that the cells are trapped there); but have the authors checked to see if CXCR3 blockade prevents the increase in ILC1s in the MAT? Finally, I understand the difficulty of underlying the spleen transplant experiment, but the n for that experiment seems quite low (so much so, that the difference in CD45.1+ ILC1s is not even significant) and I cannot find anywhere if/how many times that experiment has been repeated. As this supports a big conclusion of the paper, the authors should repeat this experiment to increase the n;
- Still regarding the migration of ILC1s to the MAT, have the authors checked if blockade of CXCR3 induces an increase in cytokine production by gd T cells? What about the inflammatory response and survival of these mice?
- Another important conclusion of the paper is that ILC1 suppression of gd-derived TNF restricts inflammation during peritonitis. Whereas by the CITE-Seq data it looks only gd T cells produce TNF (Extended Data Fig 4) the intracellular cytokine levels of TNF in gds seem very low (Fig 5g) and even the total protein levels in the MAT is the lowest when compared to all the other inflammatory markers (Fig 1e). This raises the question if suppression of gd-derived TNF mediates the regulatory role of ILC1s. The authors should formally address the role of TNF in the survival and regulation of body temperature of CLP mice, for instance by blocking TNF in the Ncr1Cre X Tbx21Flox mice;
- Is the acquisition of CD127 (and the associated regulatory phenotype, i.e. low IFNg production and PD-L1 expression) dependent only on the low IL-7 levels? If so, blocking IL-7 in naïve mice, or other inflammatory conditions that decrease IL-7 levels would also lead to the appearance of these regulatory ILC1s. Finally, do the authors have a hypothesis for how low levels of IL-7 might suppress the IFNg and increase PD-L1 expression?

Minor points:
- Bone marrow chimeras have a severe deficiency in the population of IL-17-producing gd T cells (Haas, Immunity, 2012) - which are the subset known to reside in adipose tissue. When working with populations that are not radio-resistant, a way to overcome this problem is by injecting neonatal thymocytes along adult bone marrow (Papotto, EMBO Reports, 2017). Have the authors checked that the gd population in the MAT is comparable to that from non-bone marrow chimeras? I.e., are they still able to produce IL-17 and TNF?
- How do the authors explain that PD-L1 from ILC1s induce PD1 expression in gd T cells? Could the first be secreting another cytokine/factor that increases PD1 expression instead?
- Do splenic CD127+ ILC1s also produce low levels of IFNg and express PD-L1?
- What happens to ILC1s to reach normal numbers at 24h post CLP? Do they die or do they migrate somewhere else? Have the authors performed annexing staining or checked for CD45.1+ cells in other organs from the parabiotic/transplanted mice, for instance?
- In the final point of their discussion the authors suggest that giving recombinant IL-7 could be beneficial to patients with sepsis. However, wouldn't this go against what the data shows? Reduced IL-7 induces "regulatory" ILC1s that curb inflammation during sepsis?

### Reviewer 4

This study by Nagata et al highlights the migration of ILC1s from the spleen to MAT and their interaction modulating γδ T cells via PD-1/PD-L1 during acute peritonitis. The findings contribute to further understanding of migratory behaviours in ILCs, particularly ILC1’s, and their interaction with other immune cells namely gdT cells. Here, they identified the PD-1/PD-L1 ligand-interaction as the mechanism for ILC1’s controlling gdT cell-mediated secretion of TNF and subsequent inflammation.
The mouse model Ncr/Tbx21 is compelling in demonstrating the role of ILC1 in early timepoints in this peritonitis model and represent a useful mouse model for the field. Parabiosis and splenic surgery are methodologically convincing to evidence of ILC1’s migration, further adding to the field’s understanding of circulating vs tissue resident ILCs.
While this study adds to immune cell function within AT, this reviewer suggests the following to better contextualise and support the study’s conclusions.
In determining the mechanistic crosstalk and what CD127+ PD-L1+ ILC1’s are acting on, the authors primarily pursued PD1+ gdT cells and their increased TNF production. Could other cells play a (bigger) role: There is a risk of over-simplification on immune cell crosstalk here as the authors only showed bulk CD4 and CD8 T cells not expressing PD1. Is there more data or discussion from gdT cell deficient models? More adequate analysis that other immune or T/innate-like T cell populations are not directly affected by migratory ILC1’s or express PD1 will be more convincing, using analysis on the Ncr/Tbx21 mice, or at the very least discussed.
Could TNF be a or one of many bystander effects of gdT cell activation? There is a risk of disproportionate focus on TNF from gdT cells driving this acute pathology, as they constitute a relatively minor population of ILC1’s/lymphocytes (eg <0.4% in Fig 5). Is this cytokine from gdT more critical and specific to MAT immune responses during CLP? What’s the relative contribution of total TNF increase by gdT cells against other cells? On the other hand, the critical role of TNF seems to be downplayed in significance from the start (in Fig 1) prior to pursuing the TNF-producing gdT cells. Are there further evidence or discussion on functional contribution of TNF in TNF deficient or neutralisation? Furthermore, data on longitudinal tracking of gdT cells and whether their TNF/other cytokine production significantly change towards resolution or progression across timeline post CLP could be informative.
Importantly, details on number of mice and experiments are lacking from Fig 3 onwards across manuscript and figure legends thus it is difficult to ascertain the data reproducibility and rigor.
